claim: Mermithid nematodes are obligate invertebrate parasites dating back to the Early Cretaceous.
source: Mermithid nematodes are obligate invertebrate parasites dating back to the Early Cretaceous.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to fossil records throughout the manuscript.

claim: The fossil record of mermithid nematodes is sparse, especially before the Cenozoic.
source: Their fossil record is sparse, especially before the Cenozoic, thus little is known about their early host associations.
evidence: This statement is supported by the discussion of limited pre-Cenozoic records and comparison with Cenozoic records.

claim: This study reports 16 new mermithids associated with their insect hosts from mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber.
source: This study reports 16 new mermithids associated with their insect hosts from mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber, 12 of which include previously unknown hosts.
evidence: The manuscript describes 16 specimens with detailed systematic paleontology and figures.

claim: 12 of the 16 new mermithids include previously unknown hosts.
source: This study reports 16 new mermithids associated with their insect hosts from mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber, 12 of which include previously unknown hosts.
evidence: The manuscript documents new host associations throughout the systematic descriptions.

claim: Mermithid parasitism of invertebrates was already widespread in the mid-Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystem.
source: These fossils indicate that mermithid parasitism of invertebrates was already widespread and played an important role in the mid-Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystem.
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity of hosts and number of specimens found in Kachin amber.

claim: Mermithid parasitism played an important role in the mid-Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystem.
source: These fossils indicate that mermithid parasitism of invertebrates was already widespread and played an important role in the mid-Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystem.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread nature of parasitism and known effects on host populations.

claim: Bristletails were previously unknown to be parasitized by mermithids both past and present.
source: Remarkably, three hosts (bristletails, barklice, and perforissid planthoppers) were previously unknown to be parasitized by mermithids both past and present.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and confirmed in the discussion section.

claim: Barklice were previously unknown to be parasitized by mermithids both past and present.

claim: Cretaceous nematodes including mermithids are more abundant in non-holometabolous insects compared to their Cenozoic counterparts.
source: Furthermore, our study shows that in contrast to their Cenozoic counterparts, Cretaceous nematodes including mermithids are more abundant in non-holometabolous insects.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis comparing Kachin, Baltic, and Dominican amber records.

claim: Nematodes had not completely exploited the dominant Holometabola as their hosts until the Cenozoic.
source: This result suggests that nematodes had not completely exploited the dominant Holometabola as their hosts until the Cenozoic.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of host distributions across different amber deposits.

claim: Nematodes are some of the most abundant animals on earth in terms of individuals.
source: Nematodes (roundworms), a group of non-segmented worm-like invertebrates, are some of the most abundant animals on earth in terms of individuals (Lorenzen, 1994; Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Nematodes are distributed worldwide in almost all habitats.
source: They are distributed worldwide in almost all habitats and play key roles in ecosystems by linking soil food webs, influencing plant growth and facilitating nutrient cycling (Yeates et al., 2009; van den Hoogen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ecological studies.

claim: Nematodes play key roles in ecosystems by linking soil food webs, influencing plant growth and facilitating nutrient cycling.
source: They are distributed worldwide in almost all habitats and play key roles in ecosystems by linking soil food webs, influencing plant growth and facilitating nutrient cycling (Yeates et al., 2009; van den Hoogen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to ecological studies.

claim: The earliest known definite nematode fossil occurs in the Lower Devonian Rhynie Chert inside the cortex cells of an early land plant.
source: The earliest known definite nematode fossil occurs in the Lower Devonian Rhynie Chert inside the cortex cells of an early land plant and has been considered to be a plant parasite (Poinar et al., 2008), but unconfirmed nematode-like fossils and trace fossils may date back to the Precambrian (Poinar, 1979; Parry et al., 2017; De Baets et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poinar et al., 2008.

claim: The earliest known definite nematode fossil has been considered to be a plant parasite.
source: The earliest known definite nematode fossil occurs in the Lower Devonian Rhynie Chert inside the cortex cells of an early land plant and has been considered to be a plant parasite (Poinar et al., 2008), but unconfirmed nematode-like fossils and trace fossils may date back to the Precambrian (Poinar, 1979; Parry et al., 2017; De Baets et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poinar et al., 2008.

claim: Unconfirmed nematode-like fossils and trace fossils may date back to the Precambrian.

evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple sources discussing potential Precambrian nematodes.

claim: Nematodes are exceedingly rare in the fossil record.
source: Despite their abundance in many extant ecosystems, nematodes are exceedingly rare in the fossil record, since most of them are small, with soft bodies and concealed habits (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and is consistent with known taphonomic biases.

claim: Nematodes are rare in the fossil record because most of them are small, with soft bodies and concealed habits.
source: Despite their abundance in many extant ecosystems, nematodes are exceedingly rare in the fossil record, since most of them are small, with soft bodies and concealed habits (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established taphonomic understanding.

claim: The Mermithidae represent a family of nematodes that are obligate invertebrate parasites.
source: The Mermithidae represent a family of nematodes that are obligate invertebrate parasites which occur in insects, millipedes, crustaceans, spiders, molluscs, and earthworms (Nickle, 1972; Poinar, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to taxonomic literature.

claim: Mermithids occur in insects, millipedes, crustaceans, spiders, molluscs, and earthworms.
source: The Mermithidae represent a family of nematodes that are obligate invertebrate parasites which occur in insects, millipedes, crustaceans, spiders, molluscs, and earthworms (Nickle, 1972; Poinar, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to literature on mermithid host ranges.

claim: Mermithids can affect the morphology, physiology, and even the behavior of their hosts.
source: They can affect the morphology, physiology, and even the behavior of their hosts (Petersen, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Petersen, 1985.

claim: The life cycle of mermithids comprises five stages.
source: The life cycle of mermithids comprises five stages (Poinar and Otieno, 1974; Poinar, 1983 ; Poinar, 2001b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to life cycle studies.

claim: Mermithid eggs are deposited in the environment.
source: Eggs are deposited in the environment, and the developing embryos moult once and emerge from the eggs as second-stage juveniles.
evidence: This is part of the described life cycle supported by citations.

claim: Developing mermithid embryos moult once and emerge from the eggs as second-stage juveniles.
source: Eggs are deposited in the environment, and the developing embryos moult once and emerge from the eggs as second-stage juveniles.
evidence: This is part of the described life cycle supported by citations.

claim: Second-stage juveniles are the infective stage that enter the hemocoel of potential hosts.
source: These juveniles are the infective stage that enter the hemocoel of potential hosts.
evidence: This is part of the described life cycle supported by citations.

claim: After a relatively rapid growth phase (third stage), mermithids exit hosts as postparasitic juveniles (fourth stage).
source: After a relatively rapid growth phase (third stage), mermithids exit hosts as postparasitic juveniles (fourth stage).
evidence: This is part of the described life cycle supported by citations.

claim: Postparasitic juvenile mermithids enter a quiescent phase and moult twice to become adults.
source: They then enter a quiescent phase and moult twice to become adults (Poinar, 2015a).
evidence: This is part of the described life cycle supported by citation.

claim: Mermithids tend to exit their hosts even before maturation if their hosts are stressed.
source: They tend to exit their hosts even before maturation, though, if their hosts are stressed (Poinar, 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poinar, 2015b.

claim: Hosts usually die when the mermithids exit.
source: Hosts usually die when the mermithids exit, which is why mermithids have been widely studied as possible biological control agents, especially against aquatic stages of medically important insects like mosquito larvae (Petersen, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation and is consistent with known mermithid biology.

claim: Mermithids have been widely studied as possible biological control agents, especially against aquatic stages of medically important insects like mosquito larvae.
source: Hosts usually die when the mermithids exit, which is why mermithids have been widely studied as possible biological control agents, especially against aquatic stages of medically important insects like mosquito larvae (Petersen, 1985).

claim: Mermithids are commonly considered as parasites like other nematodes, although they kill their hosts like parasitoids.
source: Although mermithids kill their hosts like parasitoids, they are commonly considered as parasites like other nematodes (De Baets et al., 2021a; De Baets et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations discussing the classification of mermithids.

claim: Palaeontological records of parasitism provide critical clues about the origination and diversification of important nematode groups.
source: Palaeontological records of parasitism provide critical clues about the origination and diversification of important nematode groups, and elucidate the synecology and coevolution of ancient parasites and their hosts.
evidence: This is a general statement about the value of paleontological research.

claim: Palaeontological records of parasitism elucidate the synecology and coevolution of ancient parasites and their hosts.
source: Palaeontological records of parasitism provide critical clues about the origination and diversification of important nematode groups, and elucidate the synecology and coevolution of ancient parasites and their hosts.
evidence: This is a general statement about the value of paleontological research.

claim: Mermithid nematodes are most likely of all nematodes to occur as recognizable fossils due to their relatively large size and invertebrate-parasitic habits.
source: Due to their relatively large size and invertebrate-parasitic habits, mermithid nematodes are most likely of all nematodes to occur as recognizable fossils, especially in amber as they exited their invertebrate hosts that became entrapped in resin (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents taphonomic reasoning.

claim: Mermithid nematodes are especially likely to occur as recognizable fossils in amber as they exited their invertebrate hosts that became entrapped in resin.
source: Due to their relatively large size and invertebrate-parasitic habits, mermithid nematodes are most likely of all nematodes to occur as recognizable fossils, especially in amber as they exited their invertebrate hosts that became entrapped in resin (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents taphonomic reasoning.

claim: The fossil record of mermithids dates back to the Early Cretaceous with Cretacimermis libani from a chironomid midge in Lebanese amber (~135 Ma).
source: Their fossil record dates back to the Early Cretaceous with Cretacimermis libani from a chironomid midge (Diptera: Chironomidae) in Lebanese amber (~135 Ma; million years ago) (Poinar et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original description.

claim: There is a dearth of examples of Cretaceous mermithids prior to the present study.
source: However, there is a dearth of examples of other Cretaceous mermithids prior to the present study, with only Cretacimermis chironomae, also from chironomid hosts, Cretacimermis protus from biting midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae) and Cretacimermis aphidophilus from an aphid (Hemiptera: Burmitaphididae) in mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber (Poinar and Buckley, 2006; Poinar and Sarto i Monteys, 2008; Poinar, 2011; Poinar, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the limited previous records.

claim: Prior to this study, only four Cretaceous mermithid species were known: Cretacimermis libani, C. chironomae, C. protus, and C. aphidophilus.
source: However, there is a dearth of examples of other Cretaceous mermithids prior to the present study, with only Cretacimermis chironomae, also from chironomid hosts, Cretacimermis protus from biting midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae) and Cretacimermis aphidophilus from an aphid (Hemiptera: Burmitaphididae) in mid-Cretaceous Kachin amber (Poinar and Buckley, 2006; Poinar and Sarto i Monteys, 2008; Poinar, 2011; Poinar, 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the list of previously known species combined with C. libani mentioned earlier.

claim: The 16 additional mermithid nematodes reported in this study triple the diversity of Cretaceous mermithids from 4 to 13 species.
source: These examples triple the diversity of Cretaceous mermithids (from 4 to 13 species) and reveal previously unknown host–parasite relationships.
evidence: This is based on counting the previously known species and the new species described.

claim: The new mermithid discoveries reveal previously unknown host–parasite relationships.
source: These examples triple the diversity of Cretaceous mermithids (from 4 to 13 species) and reveal previously unknown host–parasite relationships.
evidence: This is supported by the descriptions of new host associations in the systematic section.

claim: Mermithids were widely distributed in a number of diverse insect lineages by the mid-Cretaceous.
source: Our study also shows that mermithids were widely distributed in a number of diverse insect lineages by the mid-Cretaceous, but they preferred to parasitize non-holometabolous rather than holometabolous insects, thus providing novel insights into the early evolution of nematode parasitism of insects.
evidence: This is supported by the diversity of hosts documented in the study.

claim: Mid-Cretaceous mermithids preferred to parasitize non-holometabolous rather than holometabolous insects.
source: Our study also shows that mermithids were widely distributed in a number of diverse insect lineages by the mid-Cretaceous, but they preferred to parasitize non-holometabolous rather than holometabolous insects, thus providing novel insights into the early evolution of nematode parasitism of insects.

claim: Fossil nematodes can be attributed to the family Mermithidae based mainly on their relatively large size, coiled posture, and morphological comparison with extant mermithids.
source: Fossil nematodes can be attributed to the family Mermithidae based mainly on their relatively large size, coiled posture, and morphological comparison with extant mermithids (body shape, length, diameter, tail structure, etc.) (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to taxonomic methods.

claim: Mermithids can be distinguished from nematomorphs due to the lack of small elevations of irregular areas (areoles) on their epicuticles.
source: They can also be distinguished from nematomorphs due to the lack of small elevations of irregular areas (areoles) on their epicuticles (Poinar, 2001b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to diagnostic characters.

claim: It is impossible to place fossil mermithid nematodes in or refer them to any natural extant genus due to palaeontological inability to adequately detect all biological adult characters.
source: Due to palaeontological inability to adequately detect all biological adult characters, it is impossible to place in or refer fossil mermithid nematodes to any natural extant genus.
evidence: This represents a methodological limitation in paleontological taxonomy.

claim: Fossil collective genera have been erected for mermithids under the same guidelines as recent collective genera for difficult nematodes.
source: This is why fossil collective genera have been erected under the same guidelines as recent collective genera for difficult nematodes.
evidence: This represents a taxonomic practice for dealing with incomplete fossil material.

claim: The importance of placing nematode species in collective genera is to underpin or establish the time, place and hosts of these parasitic lineages.
source: The importance of placing nematode species in collective genera is to underpin or establish the time, place and hosts of these parasitic lineages.
evidence: This represents the rationale for the taxonomic approach used.

claim: The collective genus Cretacimermis was erected for Cretaceous Mermithidae not assignable to any previously known genus or lacking biologically preferred diagnostic characters.
source: For Cretaceous Mermithidae not assignable to any previously known genus or lacking biologically preferred diagnostic characters, the collective genus Cretacimermis was erected (but invalidly, see remarks for Cretacimermis below) (Poinar, 2001b).

claim: The genus name 'Cretacimermis' was invalidly established in Poinar, 2001b due to the lack of a formal definition.

claim: This study formally erects the genus Cretacimermis.

source: Putative hosts were determined by noting nematodes emerging from their bodies or completely emerged nematodes adjacent to potential hosts, especially if there is physical evidence that a particular insect was parasitized.

source: While the nematode has completely exited from the host, the tail end is adjacent to an exit wound on the host (Figure 2D) indicating a true parasitic association.

source: While the nematode has completely exited from the host, the tail end is adjacent to an exit wound on the host (Figure 2D) indicating a true parasitic association.

claim: Most of the body coils of Cretacimermis calypta are adjacent to the head of the adjacent damselfly, indicating that the nematode was just emerging from the host.
source: Although no exit wound can be clearly found, most of the body coils are adjacent to the head of the adjacent damselfly, indicating that the nematode was just emerging from the host.

source: The posterior part of the abdomen of the earwig has been damaged, so it is most likely that these mermithids exited from the host through this wound.

claim: Nine insect orders are now known to have been infested by mermithid nematodes in Kachin amber.
source: However, according to our new records, nine insect orders are now known to have been infested by mermithid nematodes in Kachin amber and this number is even higher than that of Baltic amber (~45 Ma) and Dominican amber (~18 Ma) (six and three insect orders, respectively), despite a much longer time spent searching for nematodes in the latter two amber deposits (Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is based on counting the distinct insect orders represented among the hosts.

claim: The number of insect orders infested by mermithids in Kachin amber (nine) is higher than that of Baltic amber (six) and Dominican amber (three).

claim: Mermithid parasitism of insects was actually widespread during the mid-Cretaceous.
source: Together with previously described mermithids in Kachin amber (Poinar, 2001b; Grimaldi et al., 2002; Poinar and Buckley, 2006; Poinar, 2011; Poinar, 2017), our results suggest that mermithid parasitism of insects was actually widespread during the mid-Cretaceous (Figure 8).
evidence: This is inferred from the diversity and abundance of mermithid-host associations found.

claim: Mermithid species are usually characterized by strong host specificity.
source: Mermithids species are usually characterized by strong host speciﬁcity, they are specific to a single species or to one or two families of insects, and are almost always lethal to their hosts (Stoffolano, 1973; Petersen, 1985), thus our study indicates that the widespread mermithid parasitism probably already played an important role in regulating the population of insects in Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mermithid host specificity.

source: Mermithids species are usually characterized by strong host speciﬁcity, they are specific to a single species or to one or two families of insects, and are almost always lethal to their hosts (Stoffolano, 1973; Petersen, 1985), thus our study indicates that the widespread mermithid parasitism probably already played an important role in regulating the population of insects in Cretaceous terrestrial ecosystems.
evidence: This is inferred from the widespread nature of parasitism and known effects on host populations.

claim: This study provides new information on fossil host–parasite associations, including three previously unknown host–mermithid associations and first fossil records of four host associations.
source: Our study provides new information on fossil host–parasite associations, including three previously unknown host–mermithid associations and first fossil records of four host associations.
evidence: This is based on comparison with known extant and fossil host associations.

claim: There are no previous extant or extinct records of nematodes attacking bristletails.
source: There are no previous extant or extinct records of nematodes attacking bristletails (Poinar, 1975; Poinar, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comprehensive reviews of nematode-host associations.

claim: No barklice are parasitized by mermithids today.
source: No barklice are parasitized by mermithids today (Poinar, 1975), but our specimens imply that such relationship might have been quite common in the mid-Cretaceous.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive review of mermithid hosts.

claim: The barklice-mermithid relationship might have been quite common in the mid-Cretaceous.
source: No barklice are parasitized by mermithids today (Poinar, 1975), but our specimens imply that such relationship might have been quite common in the mid-Cretaceous.
evidence: This is inferred from finding three different specimens of barklice parasitized by mermithids.

claim: Two members of the extinct planthopper family Perforissidae were parasitized by mermithids, providing the oldest record of mermithid parasitism of planthoppers.
source: Two members of the extinct planthopper family Perforissidae were also parasitized by mermithids, thus providing the oldest record of mermithid parasitism of planthoppers.
evidence: This is based on the age of Kachin amber and comparison with other records.

claim: The mermithid Heydenius brownii parasitized achiliid planthoppers in Baltic amber.
source: The mermithid Heydenius brownii parasitized achiliid planthoppers in Baltic amber (Poinar, 2001a) and this association also occurs in extant planthoppers (Choo et al., 1989; Helden, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the fossil record.

claim: Mermithid parasitism of planthoppers also occurs in extant planthoppers.
source: The mermithid Heydenius brownii parasitized achiliid planthoppers in Baltic amber (Poinar, 2001a) and this association also occurs in extant planthoppers (Choo et al., 1989; Helden, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of extant associations.

claim: The findings are the first fossil records of mermithids parasitizing dragonflies (Odonata), earwigs (Dermaptera), crickets (Orthoptera) and cockroaches (Blattodea).
source: Furthermore, our findings are the first fossil records of mermithids parasitizing dragonflies (Odonata), earwigs (Dermaptera), crickets (Orthoptera) and cockroaches (Blattodea), four host associations predicted from extant records (Poinar, 1975).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously known fossil records.

claim: Mermithid parasitism of dragonflies, earwigs, crickets and cockroaches are four host associations predicted from extant records.

evidence: This is supported by citation to a comprehensive review of extant associations.

claim: Not only the mermithids, but also the nematodes as a whole, experienced a certain degree of host transition between the Cretaceous and Cenozoic.
source: Our results indicate that not only the mermithids, but also the nematodes as a whole, experienced a certain degree of host transition between the Cretaceous and Cenozoic (Figure 9).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of host distributions across time periods.

claim: The influence of collection bias on the observed host patterns is probably low because Kachin amber has been extensively studied in the last two decades.
source: We cannot fully exclude the possibility of collection bias, but its influence is probably low because Kachin amber has been extensively studied in the last two decades and its biota has already become the most diverse known amber biota; moreover, holometabolous insects are much more diverse in the collections than non-holometabolous ones (1296 vs 465 species: Ross, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the diversity of Kachin amber biota.

claim: The Kachin amber biota has already become the most diverse known amber biota.
source: We cannot fully exclude the possibility of collection bias, but its influence is probably low because Kachin amber has been extensively studied in the last two decades and its biota has already become the most diverse known amber biota; moreover, holometabolous insects are much more diverse in the collections than non-holometabolous ones (1296 vs 465 species: Ross, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ross, 2023.

claim: Holometabolous insects are much more diverse in Kachin amber collections than non-holometabolous ones (1296 vs 465 species).

evidence: This is supported by citation to Ross, 2023.

claim: It is unlikely that holometabolous insects are underrepresented among the known hosts of mermithids in Kachin amber.
source: It is therefore unlikely that holometabolous insects are underrepresented among the known hosts of mermithids.
evidence: This is inferred from the high diversity of holometabolous insects in collections.

claim: Among the insect hosts of mermithids preserved in Kachin amber, only one of the nine orders (Diptera) is holometabolous.
source: Among the insect hosts of mermithids preserved in Kachin amber, only one of the nine orders (Diptera) is holometabolous (i.e. insects with 'complete' metamorphosis), whilst it is four out of six (Hymenoptera, Trichoptera, Lepidoptera and Diptera) in Baltic amber and all three insect host orders (Hymenoptera, Coleoptera and Diptera) are holometabolous in Dominican amber.
evidence: This is based on counting the holometabolous orders among the hosts.

claim: In Baltic amber, four out of six insect orders hosting mermithids are holometabolous (Hymenoptera, Trichoptera, Lepidoptera and Diptera).

evidence: This is based on counting the holometabolous orders among the hosts.

claim: Most dipteran larvae develop in moist or aquatic environments that are particularly suitable habitats for nematodes.

claim: Holometabola are the most important hosts of extant mermithids as well as all invertebrate-parasitizing nematodes.
source: It is evident that Holometabola are the most important hosts of extant mermithids as well as all invertebrate-parasitizing nematodes (Poinar, 1975) and this hexapod subgroup dominated the insect fauna during the Cretaceous (Labandeira and Sepkoski, 1993; Labandeira, 2005; Sohn et al., 2015; Peters et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poinar, 1975.
